notes.meaning: Saul's father Kish is introduced as a wealthy and influential man from the tribe of Benjamin. Benjamin was the smallest tribe in Israel, having suffered terrible losses during an earlier civil war. Even so, God was preparing to choose Israel's very first king from this modest background.

Saul is described as an unusually tall and handsome young man, standing a full head taller than anyone around him. The people had asked for a king like the surrounding nations, and Saul looked every bit the part of a royal champion. Scripture focuses here on his striking physical appearance rather than his spiritual devotion.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that Saul is the only Israelite whose great height is highlighted in Scripture, mirroring the way biblical writers usually describe intimidating foreign warriors.

notes.meaning: Kish loses some of his female donkeys and sends Saul along with a family servant to find them. In that era, donkeys were valuable working animals used for riding and carrying heavy loads. God used this ordinary, frustrating family chore to direct Saul toward his royal destiny.

Saul and his servant hike through several hilly regions and territories without finding the lost herd. Saul showed patient obedience to his father by pursuing the search through difficult terrain. Though the journey seemed completely wasted, God was quietly steering their footsteps toward the prophet Samuel.

When they reach the district of Zuph, Saul suggests heading home so his father will not begin worrying about their safety. He shows thoughtful care for his parent by putting his father's peace of mind above the lost livestock. This caring decision brought them right outside the town where Samuel was staying.

The servant suggests visiting a respected man of God in the nearby city who might tell them which way to search. Samuel had a well-known reputation throughout Israel because everything he spoke from God came true. Saul and his helper turned to him for practical advice about lost property, unaware of God's larger purpose.

Saul hesitates because their travel rations are gone and they have no gift to offer the prophet. In ancient Near Eastern culture, approaching a leader or prophet without a small present was considered bad manners. Saul was not trying to bribe Samuel, but wanted to show proper respect.

The servant discovers that he has a quarter of a silver shekel in hand to give to the man of God. This small coin was a modest amount, but it served as a fitting token of honor. With this practical problem solved, they decide to visit the prophet.

A brief explanation notes that in earlier days people used the title 'seer' when asking for guidance from God. The word pointed to a person granted spiritual vision to perceive what ordinary eyes could not see. Over time, the title 'prophet' became the customary term used across the nation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars generally regard this parenthetical explanation as a note added by a later compiler to explain an archaic term to later readers.

notes.meaning: Saul welcomes the servant's idea and agrees that they should enter the town where the man of God is staying. His willingness to listen to his servant shows a helpful sense of humility. Together they set out toward the city where Saul's life would change forever.

While walking up the hill toward the town gate, they meet young women coming out to draw water from the well. Wells were normally situated outside the city walls, making them busy community gathering places. Saul takes the opportunity to ask them whether the seer is present in the town.

The young women answer that Samuel has just arrived to oversee a community sacrifice and feast at the town's high place. A high place was an elevated outdoor spot used for prayer and worship before the central temple was built in Jerusalem. The timing was arranged so that Saul would arrive on the very day of this sacred gathering.

The women urge them to hurry because the invited guests will not eat until Samuel arrives to bless the sacrificial meal. Asking God to bless the food was an important part of sharing a fellowship meal with the Lord. This ancient practice of praying over food became the pattern for giving thanks before meals today.

Saul and his servant walk up into the city and meet Samuel coming toward them on his way to the high place. Samuel wore no royal robes or special entourage, appearing just like an ordinary citizen. Yet God's providence brought the two men together at the exact minute planned.

The day before Saul arrived, the Lord had privately spoken to Samuel about what would take place. The Hebrew phrase literally says God uncovered Samuel's ear, picturing someone gently moving hair aside to whisper a secret. God prepared His prophet ahead of time so he would recognize the new leader immediately.

God instructed Samuel to anoint the incoming traveler as a military leader to deliver Israel from Philistine oppression. Even though the Israelites had sinned by demanding an earthly king, God showed deep mercy by hearing their cries of distress. He provided a commander who would defend His people from their enemies.

When Samuel catches sight of Saul, the Lord confirms that this tall stranger is the man He promised to send. Samuel may have wondered in his own thoughts if this newcomer was the chosen leader, and God answered his silent question. God directed the prophet step by step as the encounter unfolded.

Saul approaches Samuel in the city gateway and asks where the seer's house is located, not realizing who he is addressing. Samuel did not carry himself with proud displays of authority, making him easy to approach. God often works through faithful servants who do not call attention to themselves.

Samuel reveals that he is the seer and invites Saul to walk ahead of him up to the feast. He tells Saul to eat with him that day and promises to answer everything on his mind the next morning. By giving Saul the place of honor, Samuel began treating him as the future leader of the nation.

Samuel reassures Saul that the donkeys lost three days earlier have already been found, proving his supernatural insight. He then hints that all the hopes and longings of Israel are resting on Saul and his father's household. This mysterious remark pointed directly to the royal office Saul was about to receive.

Saul replies with genuine surprise, asking why Samuel would say such great things to someone from the smallest tribe and a minor family. Benjamin had been nearly wiped out in past generations, and Saul considered his family unworthy of royal honor. In these early days, Saul displayed real modesty and humility about his position.

Samuel leads Saul and his servant into the dining hall and places them in the chief seats among thirty invited town leaders. Seating positions at ancient sacred banquets were carefully chosen to reflect honor, and placing Saul next to the host signaled his high importance. The local leaders were thus prepared to see this stranger elevated above them.

Samuel orders the cook to bring out a special portion of meat that he had instructed him to reserve earlier. This showed that Samuel had planned for this particular guest before Saul even reached the town. God's plan had been arranged in advance right down to the food on the table.

The cook sets the roasted leg before Saul, and Samuel invites him to eat the special portion preserved for him. The upper leg was traditionally considered the best portion of the animal, often reserved for priests and guests of honor. Presenting this portion to Saul symbolized the heavy burden of leadership being placed upon his shoulders.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the Hebrew phrasing points to the cook speaking part of this invitation, explaining to Saul how the reserved meat was kept specifically for his arrival.

notes.meaning: After the feast ends, Samuel takes Saul down into the city and talks with him on the flat roof of the house. Rooftops in that part of the world provided a private, quiet place away from household activity. Samuel used this uninterrupted time to prepare Saul's mind for the spiritual responsibilities of ruling Israel.

At dawn the next morning, Samuel calls Saul awake where he had been sleeping on the rooftop. They rise together and walk through the town toward the road leading home. Samuel was preparing to share God's private message away from the hearing of the townspeople.

As they reach the edge of the city, Samuel tells Saul to send his servant ahead so they can stand alone. Samuel wanted Saul to hear the divine calling directly without any distractions. This quiet moment set the stage for Samuel to pour the sacred oil over Saul as Israel's new king.
